II

One evening as I was lying flat on the deck of my steamboat, I heard voices approaching—and there were the nephew and the uncle strolling along the bank. I had nearly lost myself in a doze, when somebody said in my ear, as it were: ‘I am as harmless as a little child, but I don’t like to be dictated to. Am I the manager—or am I not? I was ordered to send him there. It’s incredible.’ ... They were standing on the shore alongside the forepart of the steamboat. ‘He has asked the Administration to be sent there,’ said the other, ‘with the idea of showing what he could do; and I was instructed accordingly. Look at the influence that man must have. Is it not frightful?’ ‘The climate may do away with this difficulty for you. Is he alone there?’ ‘Yes,’ answered the manager; ‘he sent his assistant down the river with a note to me… “Clear this poor devil out of the country… I had rather be alone…”’ ‘Anything since then?’ ‘Ivory,’ jerked the nephew; ‘lots of it—prime sort—lots—most annoying, from him.’ … They had been talking about Kurtz.

They were astounded that, after sending down ivory by a fleet of canoes with an English half-caste, Kurtz himself, after coming three hundred miles, had turned back alone in a small dugout with four paddlers—towards the depths of the wilderness, towards his empty and desolate station. His name had not been pronounced; he was ‘that man.’ The half-caste, who had conducted a difficult trip with great prudence and pluck, was invariably ‘that scoundrel.’ They strolled and whispered, then: ‘We will not be free from unfair competition till one of these fellows is hanged for an example.’—‘Certainly—get him hanged! Why not? Anything—anything can be done in this country. That’s what I say; nobody here, you understand, here, can endanger your position. And why? You stand the climate—you outlast them all. The danger is in Europe; but there before I left I took care to—’ Presently the uncle, with a short flipper of an arm, made a gesture that took in the forest, the creek, the mud, the river—seemed to beckon with a dishonouring flourish before the sunlit face of the land a treacherous appeal to the lurking death, to the hidden evil, to the profound darkness of its heart. The high stillness confronted these two with its ominous patience.

In a few days the Eldorado Expedition went into the patient wilderness, that closed upon it as the sea closes over a diver. Long afterwards the news came that all the donkeys were dead. I was then excited at the prospect of meeting Kurtz very soon. When I say very soon I mean it comparatively. It was just two months from the day we left the creek when we came to the bank below Kurtz’s station.

Going up that river was like traveling back to the earliest beginnings of the world, when vegetation rioted on the earth and the big trees were kings. An empty stream, a great silence, an impenetrable forest. The air was warm, thick, heavy, sluggish. The long stretches of the waterway ran on, deserted, into the gloom of overshadowed distances. On silvery sand-banks hippos and alligators sunned themselves side by side. We butted all day long against shoals, trying to find the channel, till you thought yourself bewitched and cut off for ever from everything you had known once—somewhere—far away—in another existence perhaps. This stillness of life did not in the least resemble a peace. It was the stillness of an implacable force brooding over an inscrutable intention. I watched for sunken stones; shaved by a fluke some infernal sly old snag; hunted dead wood for next day’s steaming. When you have to attend to things of that sort, the reality—the reality, I tell you—fades. The inner truth is hidden—luckily, luckily.

“Try to be civil, Marlow,” growled a voice.

“I beg your pardon… After all, I managed not to sink that steamboat on my first trip… We had enlisted some of the cannibals for a crew. Fine fellows—in their place. They did not eat each other before my face: they had brought along a provision of hippo-meat which went rotten, and made the mystery of the wilderness stink in my nostrils. The word ivory would ring in the air at the stations—and on we went, like a sluggish beetle crawling on the floor of a lofty portico. For me it crawled towards Kurtz—exclusively. We penetrated deeper and deeper into the heart of darkness. At night sometimes the roll of drums would run up the river and remain sustained faintly… We were wanderers on a prehistoric earth… We glided past like phantoms, wondering and secretly appalled… We could not remember because we were travelling in the night of first ages, of those ages that are gone, leaving hardly a sign—and no memories.

The earth seemed unearthly. We are accustomed to look upon the shackled form of a conquered monster, but there—there you could look at a thing monstrous and free. It was unearthly, and the men were—No, they were not inhuman… what thrilled you was just the thought of their humanity—like yours—the thought of your remote kinship with this wild and passionate uproar… truth—truth stripped of its cloak of time. He must meet that truth with his own true stuff… Principles won’t do… No; you want a deliberate belief. An appeal to me in this fiendish row—is there? Very well; I hear… But I had no time. I had to mess about with white-lead and strips of woolen blanket on the leaky steam-pipes… And between whiles I had to look after the savage who was fireman—an improved specimen; he could fire up a vertical boiler. To look at him was as edifying as seeing a dog in a parody of breeches… He was useful because he had been instructed; and what he knew was this—that should the water disappear, the evil spirit inside the boiler would get angry and take a terrible vengeance. So he sweated and fired up and watched the glass fearfully, while the wooded banks slipped past—and we crept on, towards Kurtz.

Some fifty miles below the Inner Station we came upon a hut of reeds, an inclined and melancholy pole with the tatters of a flag, and a neatly stacked wood-pile. On the stack a flat piece of board: ‘Wood for you. Hurry up. Approach cautiously.’ A torn curtain of red twill hung in the doorway; the dwelling was dismantled; and by the door I picked up a book—An Inquiry into some Points of Seamanship—sixty years old, back stitched afresh with white cotton thread. The humble pages were luminous with another than a professional light. But in the margin were notes pencilled—cipher, I thought. Fancy a man lugging such a book into this nowhere—and making notes—in cipher at that! I slipped the book into my pocket.

The current was more rapid; the steamer at her last gasp. I fretted and fumed and argued with myself whether I would talk openly with Kurtz; but any action of mine would be a mere futility. Towards the evening of the second day we judged ourselves eight miles from Kurtz’s station. The manager, grave, advised waiting for daylight, and—if we were to approach cautiously—to approach by day. I brought up in the middle of the stream. Dusk glided in; then a white fog, very warm and clammy… It lifted as a shutter lifts—then down again. I ordered the chain paid out. A very loud cry, as of infinite desolation, soared slowly in the opaque air. It culminated in intolerable shrieking—then stopped—leaving us stiffened and listening to the nearly as appalling silence.

We hauled the chain short, ready to trip the anchor. ‘Will they attack?’—‘We will be all butchered in this fog,’ murmured another. The whites were shocked by such an outrageous row; the black fellows quiet, alert. Their headman, with fierce nostrils and oily ringlets, said: ‘Catch ’im. Give ’im to us.’—‘To you? what would you do with them?’—‘Eat ’im!’ He and his chaps must have been very hungry. Every week they had three pieces of brass wire about nine inches long—theory: to buy provisions. You can see how that worked. Why in the name of all the gnawing devils of hunger they didn’t go for us—they were thirty to five—amazes me now. Restraint! What possible restraint?… No fear can stand up to hunger… and as to superstition, beliefs, and what you may call principles, they are less than chaff in a breeze. Yet there was the fact—the fact dazzling—like a ripple on an unfathomable enigma.

The manager, with his beautiful resignation, muttered of going on at once. ‘I authorize you to take all the risks.’—‘I refuse to take any,’ said I. The approach to this Kurtz grubbing for ivory was beset by as many dangers as though he had been an enchanted princess in a fabulous castle. ‘Will they attack, do you think?’ he asked. I did not think so. The thick fog was one; no canoes visible; but chiefly the nature of the cries—an irresistible impression of sorrow. What we afterwards alluded to as an attack was really an attempt at repulse… purely protective.

It developed, two hours after the fog lifted, about a mile and a half below the station. We floundered round a bend and opened a reach with a chain of shallow patches down midstream. I headed for the western passage. It was narrower than I had supposed; to the right a high, steep bank overgrown; a strip of shadow on the water. Very slowly, as you may imagine, I sheered her inshore—the water deeper there. Then my poleman stretched himself flat; the fireman sat abruptly; sticks were flying—whizzing before my nose, pattering. Arrows, by Jove! I stepped in to close the shutter on the landside. I saw a face amongst the leaves, fierce and steady; then, as though a veil had been removed, naked breasts, arms, legs, glaring eyes—the bush swarming with human limbs glistening of bronze colour. ‘Steer her straight,’ I said. The helmsman, all swagger gone, foamed a little; he flung the shutter open and let off the Martini-Henry. No room to turn; a snag somewhere ahead in smoke; so I crowded her into the bank—right into the bank, where I knew the water was deep.

We tore along the overhanging bushes; the fusillade stopped when the squirts got empty. Something big appeared before the shutter; the rifle went overboard; the man stepped back, looked at me with an extraordinary, profound, familiar manner, and fell upon my feet. The shaft of a spear had caught him in the side; my shoes were full; a pool of blood lay very still. With one hand I jerked the steam whistle—screech after screech. The tumult of yells was checked; then from the depths of the woods went out such a tremulous and prolonged wail of mournful fear and utter despair as may be imagined to follow the flight of the last hope from the earth… then silence, and the languid beat of the stern-wheel. The pilgrim in pink pyjamas appeared; we two whites stood over the helmsman. He died without a sound. ‘Can you steer?’ I made him steer; to tell you the truth, I was morbidly anxious to change my shoes and socks. ‘He is dead,’ murmured the fellow. ‘No doubt about it,’ said I… ‘And by the way, I suppose Mr. Kurtz is dead as well by this time.’

I flung one shoe overboard, and became aware that that was exactly what I had been looking forward to—a talk with Kurtz. The man presented himself as a voice… ‘Now I will never hear him.’ The other shoe went flying unto the devil-god of that river. ‘By Jove! it’s all over… the gift has vanished…’ My sorrow had a startling extravagance.

There was a pause of profound stillness, then a match flared—my lean face appeared, worn, hollow. “Absurd!” I cried. “This is the worst of trying to tell… And you say, Absurd! Absurd be—exploded!… I was cut to the quick at the idea of having lost the inestimable privilege of listening to the gifted Kurtz. Of course I was wrong. The privilege was waiting for me… A voice. He was very little more than a voice.”

Poor fool of a helmsman! If he had only left that shutter alone. He had no restraint—just like Kurtz—a tree swayed by the wind. I dragged him out and tipped him overboard. The pilgrims murmured; my friends the wood-cutters were likewise scandalized—for a better, inadmissible reason. I had made up my mind that if my late helmsman was to be eaten, the fishes alone should have him. They had given up Kurtz—given up the station; Kurtz was dead, the station burnt. The red-haired pilgrim danced at the thought of a glorious slaughter. ‘You made a glorious lot of smoke, anyhow,’ said I. The retreat, I maintained—and I was right—was caused by the screeching of the steam whistle.

A clearing showed on the bank; on the hill a long decaying building; near it half-a-dozen slim posts remained in a row, roughly trimmed, their upper ends ornamented with round carved balls. On the waterside a white man under a hat like a cart-wheel beckoned with his whole arm. We steamed past, stopped the engines, and drifted down. ‘We have been attacked,’ screamed the manager. ‘I know—I know. It’s all right,’ yelled back the other. His aspect reminded me of a harlequin. His clothes were covered with bright patches—blue, red, and yellow; a beardless, boyish face; little blue eyes; sunshine and shadow chasing each other. ‘You English?’ he asked. ‘Never mind! Are we in time?’—‘He is up there,’ with a toss up the hill, his face overcast and bright by turns.

When the manager and pilgrims, armed to the teeth, had gone to the house, this chap came aboard. ‘They are simple people,’ he repeated; ‘keep enough steam to blow the whistle.’ ‘Don’t you talk with Mr. Kurtz?’ I said. ‘You don’t talk with that man—you listen to him,’ he exclaimed. In a twinkling he sank, then jumped up, seized both my hands—‘Brother sailor… Russian… son of an arch-priest… What? Tobacco!’ The pipe soothed him. He had run away, wandered nearly two years alone. He had persuaded a Dutchman, old Van Shuyten, to fit him out; sent him one small lot of ivory ‘so he can’t call me a little thief.’ ‘I had some wood stacked for you. That was my old house. Did you see?’ I gave him Towson’s book. ‘The only book I had left…’ He thumbed the pages. ‘You made notes in Russian?’—He nodded. I had thought cipher. He had had lots of trouble to keep these people off. ‘Why did they attack us?’—He hesitated: ‘They don’t want him to go.’ He nodded, full of mystery and wisdom. ‘I tell you,’ he cried, ‘this man has enlarged my mind.’

…Later—listen—you must hear the rest as it came to me. The wilderness had patted him on the head, and, behold, it was like a ball—an ivory ball; it had caressed him, and—lo!—he had withered; it had taken him, loved him, embraced him, got into his veins, consumed his flesh, and sealed his soul to its own by the inconceivable ceremonies of some devilish initiation. Ivory? Heaps of it, stacks of it. The old mud shanty was bursting with it. ‘Mostly fossil,’ the manager had said; but we filled the steamboat with it, and had to pile a lot on the deck. You should have heard him say, ‘My ivory.’ ‘My Intended, my ivory, my station, my river, my—’ everything belonged to him… The thing was to know what he belonged to, how many powers of darkness claimed him for their own. He had taken a high seat amongst the devils of the land—I mean literally.

All Europe contributed to the making of Kurtz; the International Society for the Suppression of Savage Customs had intrusted him with the making of a report. He had written it—seventeen pages of close writing—eloquent, vibrating with eloquence. He began with the argument that we whites, from the point of development we had arrived at, ‘must necessarily appear to them [savages] in the nature of supernatural beings—we approach them with the might of a deity’… ‘By the simple exercise of our will we can exert a power for good practically unbounded’… The peroration was magnificent… It gave me the notion of an exotic Immensity ruled by an august Benevolence. There were no practical hints—unless a kind of note at the foot of the last page, scrawled much later, in an unsteady hand, may be regarded as the exposition of a method: ‘Exterminate all the brutes!’

He had apparently forgotten that valuable postscriptum; later, when he in a sense came to himself, he entreated me to take good care of ‘my pamphlet.’ Whatever he was, he was not common. He had the power to charm or frighten rudimentary souls; to fill the small souls of the pilgrims with misgivings; he had one devoted friend at least; and he had conquered one soul that was neither rudimentary nor tainted with self-seeking. No; I can’t forget him, though I am not prepared to affirm the fellow was exactly worth the life we lost in getting to him. I missed my late helmsman awfully. He had steered for me; I had to look after him; a subtle bond had been created; and the intimate profundity of that look he gave me when he received his hurt remains to this day in my memory—like a claim of distant kinship affirmed in a supreme moment.

I tell you, the earth for us is a place to live in… and there your strength comes in—your power of devotion to an obscure, back-breaking business. I am not trying to excuse or even explain—I am trying to account to myself for—for—Mr. Kurtz—for the shade of Mr. Kurtz. This initiated wraith from the back of Nowhere honoured me with its amazing confidence because it could speak English to me… And I—later—I laid the ghost of his gifts at last with a lie. Girl? Did I mention a girl? ‘My Intended.’ They—the women—are out of it—should be out of it. But that is for later. For now, he was very little more than a voice.
